title: 8. Looking after it
text:
Status: draft. Facts checked against Nectar support and tutorial pages, October 2026.

A VM is yours to run: nobody patches it, backs it up, or tidies it away for you. This page covers the routine jobs.


Placeholders: <username> is a Linux account on the VM; <server> is the instance name.


sudo adduser <username>
This creates the home directory and prompts for a password. The password is what they use for RStudio Server (06).
Nectar images turn off SSH password login (PasswordAuthentication no), so for SSH each user needs a key (nectar-images ssh role):

They run ssh-keygen -t ed25519 on their own computer and send you the public key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub). Never accept or send a private key.
You install it:
sudo mkdir -p /home/<username>/.ssh
echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... them@laptop' | sudo tee -a /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chown -R <username>:<username> /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo chmod 700 /home/<username>/.ssh
sudo chmod 600 /home/<username>/.ssh/authorized_keys
They log in with ssh <username>@<ip>.

To give access to a shared data directory, add them to its group (05): sudo usermod -aG lab <username> (takes effect at their next login).



sudo lets a user do anything, including read everyone’s files and break the machine. Keep it to the one or two people who administer the VM:
sudo usermod -aG sudo <username>     # grant
sudo deluser <username> sudo         # revoke
getent group sudo                    # who has it
Most users never need it: R packages install into their own library, and containers can be run for them.



sudo passwd <username>        # set a new password (e.g. they forgot it)
sudo passwd -e <username>     # force a change at next login
Users change their own with passwd. Send temporary passwords by a different channel from the username.




Copy off anything worth keeping from /home/<username> and their files on volumes (sudo find /mnt/data -user <username>).
Remove the account and home directory:
sudo deluser --remove-home <username>
To lock an account without deleting it: sudo usermod -L -e 1 <username>.







Official Nectar Ubuntu and Debian images ship with unattended-upgrades enabled, installing security updates only, daily (nectar-images unattended-upgrades role). Check:
cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades
# APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";
sudo unattended-upgrades --dry-run -v | head
If it’s missing (another image, or you turned it off):
sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades    # answer Yes
It does not reboot the VM for you.



Do this every month or so, and before installing anything big:
sudo apt update
sudo apt full-upgrade
sudo apt autoremove
full-upgrade is like upgrade but may also add or remove packages to complete an upgrade (typical for new kernels). Read what it proposes to remove before saying yes.



Kernel and core library updates only take effect after a reboot:
cat /var/run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null       # exists if a reboot is needed
cat /var/run/reboot-required.pkgs 2>/dev/null  # which packages asked for it
Warn your users, then sudo reboot. Volumes in /etc/fstab remount automatically (05); check with df -h afterwards.
R and Python packages are not touched by apt unless installed from it; see 07.




Every running instance uses Service Units (SU) per hour, and a shut-off instance still uses SU. Only shelving or deleting it stops the meter (SU and usage).
If the VM will be idle for weeks, shelve it:
openstack server shelve <server>
openstack server unshelve <server>   # when you need it again
or Project → Compute → Instances → Shelve Instance.
Shelving snapshots the root disk and frees the hypervisor. Attached volumes and object storage are untouched. Unshelving takes a few minutes, longer for big disks. TODO(verify): whether a Classic Provider instance keeps its public IP across shelve/unshelve; if not, update its DNS record (06).





An instance snapshot is an image of the root disk only, not attached volumes (Nectar tutorial). Take one before risky changes (a release upgrade, a big reconfiguration):
openstack server image create --name <server>-2026-10-29 <server>
openstack image list --private
You can launch a new instance from it (Launch Instance → Source: Instance Snapshot).



A volume snapshot uses volume quota equal to the volume’s size, and a volume can’t be deleted while it has snapshots (Nectar tutorial).
openstack volume snapshot create --volume <volname> --force <volname>-2026-10-29
For real backups of data, use the volume backup service or copy to object storage (05).



E.g. to give a colleague’s project a copy of your set-up, or to move to a new allocation (image sharing):

You (owner):
openstack image set --shared <image>
openstack image add project <image> <their-project-id>
(The older form is glance member-create <image-id> <project-id>.)
They accept it, from their project:
openstack image set --accept <image-id>

It then shows in their image list. Shared snapshots survive the deletion of your project at allocation expiry (expiry).



A snapshot is a frozen machine: old OS, old packages, and nobody remembers what was done to it. A script records what you did and can be re-run on a fresh, current image.

Keep your setup as a script in git (e.g. setup.sh: apt install lines, R/Python installs, users, fstab entries, nginx config).
Each time you do something by hand on the VM, add it to the script.
Test it now and then by launching a fresh VM and running it.
You can pass the script as a Customization Script (user data) when you launch an instance, and cloud-init runs it at first boot.

Then a snapshot is just a convenience, and losing the VM costs you an hour, not a month.




Inside the VM, OpenStack’s metadata service tells you about the instance (OpenStack metadata docs):
# the Customization Script (user data) you launched with
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/openstack/latest/user_data

# instance name, UUID, availability zone, keypair, project ID
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/openstack/latest/meta_data.json | python3 -m json.tool

# network configuration
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/openstack/latest/network_data.json | python3 -m json.tool
The older EC2-style paths (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, .../latest/user-data) still work. These addresses only answer from inside the instance.
Handy in scripts, e.g. to find the availability zone before creating a volume:
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/openstack/latest/meta_data.json \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["availability_zone"])'



Allocations last up to 12 months. As expiry approaches you get warnings, then quota drops to zero, then instances are stopped, snapshotted and terminated, and finally everything is deleted. See 02 for the timeline and how to extend, and the Nectar expiry article. Submitting an extension request pauses the process.
Don’t rely on the automatic clean-up. To hand back cleanly:

Tell your users and agree a date.
Copy data off: from volumes and home directories to object storage, your institution’s storage, or another project. Check the copy (rclone check, file counts, sizes).
Save the recipe: make sure your setup script and any config (nginx, fstab, crontab) are in git.
Delete instances: Project → Compute → Instances → Delete, or openstack server delete <server>.
Delete volume snapshots, then volumes:
openstack volume snapshot list
openstack volume snapshot delete <snapshot>
openstack volume list
openstack volume delete <volname>
Delete instance snapshots you no longer need (openstack image list --private, openstack image delete <image>), and stop sharing any you shared.
Empty object storage you no longer need (rclone purge nectar_s3:my-bucket, or swift delete <container>). Public containers survive project deletion, so don’t leave data public by accident.
Release DNS records so the names don’t point at an IP someone else may get:
openstack recordset list <project>.cloud.edu.au.
openstack recordset delete <project>.cloud.edu.au. <server>.<project>.cloud.edu.au.
If you used your own domain, remove its records at your DNS provider.
Revoke credentials: openstack ec2 credentials delete <access>, and delete application credentials (Identity → Application Credentials).
Tell the node or support you’re done, if the allocation is still running. TODO(verify): whether there is a formal “close allocation” step in the dashboard.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
Status: draft. Source: legacy/openstack/create_install_rstudio_openstack.md and issue #14, updated against current docs (October 2026).

The goal is RStudio Server at https://<server>.<project>.cloud.edu.au, not http://<ip>:8787. Without HTTPS, passwords and data cross the network in clear text.
The arrangement is:
browser ──HTTPS:443──> nginx (on the VM) ──HTTP──> RStudio Server on 127.0.0.1:8787
nginx holds the certificate and talks to the outside world. RStudio Server only listens on the VM itself.


If you don’t need full control, let Nectar do the setup. In the dashboard, the Applications tab has a Quick Deploy option for R-Studio. It launches a VM with RStudio Server and Shiny Server already installed. If you choose a DNS zone during the deploy, you get automatic HTTPS at https://<host>.<project>.cloud.edu.au. You can also add a volume, which must be in the same availability zone as the VM (Nectar support: R-Studio application, tutorial: configuring applications).
Each deploy creates its own security group. Delete these when you delete the application, or they pile up (Nectar support: application security groups).
The rest of this page is the do-it-yourself route: more steps, but you choose the versions, the configuration and what else runs on the machine.
Placeholders used below:








Placeholder
Meaning
Example




<project>
your Nectar project name, which is also your DNS zone
myproject


<server>
the hostname you choose for this VM
rstudio


<ip>
the VM’s public IP address (dashboard: Project → Compute → Instances)
203.0.113.10


<fqdn>
<server>.<project>.cloud.edu.au
rstudio.myproject.cloud.edu.au


<username>
a user account on the VM
alice







A running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS VM you can SSH into as ubuntu (04). Ubuntu 26.04 LTS is supported by CRAN and Posit, so it should work the same way. TODO(verify): whether Nectar currently offers an official Ubuntu 26.04 image.
Your project has an allocation. Nectar creates a DNS zone named after the project (<project>.cloud.edu.au.) for new and renewed allocations (Nectar DNS service).




Follow CRAN’s Ubuntu instructions. On the VM:
sudo apt update -qq
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends software-properties-common dirmngr
wget -qO- https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/marutter_pubkey.asc \
  | sudo tee -a /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc
# optional: fingerprint should be E298A3A825C0D65DFD57CBB651716619E084DAB9
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc
sudo add-apt-repository "deb https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs)-cran40/"
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends r-base r-base-dev
$(lsb_release -cs) fills in your release (noble for 24.04, resolute for 26.04). For geospatial libraries and binary packages, see 07.



Get the current Ubuntu .deb from Posit’s download page (it currently redirects to docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html). The one package, built on jammy, is for Ubuntu 22, 24 and 26. Don’t copy a version number from old notes: the filename changes with every release.
Either copy the link from that page, or use Posit’s “latest stable” redirect and check which version it points to:
curl -sI https://rstudio.org/download/latest/stable/server/jammy/rstudio-server-latest-amd64.deb | grep -i ^location
Then download and install it (in October 2026 the current file was rstudio-server-2026.10.1-239-amd64.deb):
wget https://rstudio.org/download/latest/stable/server/jammy/rstudio-server-latest-amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./rstudio-server-latest-amd64.deb
sudo systemctl status rstudio-server
apt install ./file.deb pulls in dependencies, so you no longer need gdebi. TODO(verify): the rstudio.org/download/latest/... redirect is not documented on Posit’s download page, though it worked when this was written. If it stops working, copy the link from the download page instead.



nginx will be the only way in, so tell RStudio Server not to listen on the public interface (Posit: running with a proxy):
echo "www-address=127.0.0.1" | sudo tee -a /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf
sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server
Check it:
sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8787
You should see 127.0.0.1:8787, not 0.0.0.0:8787.



You do this with the OpenStack command-line client and its DNS (Designate) plugin. It can run on any machine, such as your laptop or the VM itself.


Use a venv rather than apt install python3-openstackclient. The apt packages can lag behind and mixing them with system Python caused trouble before (see issue #14). Ubuntu 24.04 also refuses pip install outside a venv.
sudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip
python3 -m venv ~/venvs/openstack
source ~/venvs/openstack/bin/activate
pip install python-openstackclient python-designateclient
When you come back later, run source ~/venvs/openstack/bin/activate again first. References: Nectar: OpenStack client, Python venv docs.



Do either of the following.
Application credential (preferred for anything scripted or left on a machine). In the Nectar dashboard, select the right project, then go to Identity → Application Credentials, create one, and download its openrc file. It is tied to one project, can be revoked, and doesn’t expose your personal password (Nectar: application credentials, using them).
# clear any leftover OS_* variables first, e.g. open a fresh shell
source app-cred-<name>-openrc.sh
Project OpenStack RC file. In the dashboard, select the project, click your email address (top right), and choose “OpenStack RC File”. You’ll be asked for your OpenStack password. This is not your institutional login: generate it under Settings → Reset Password (Nectar: credentials).
source <project>-openrc.sh
Never commit either file, or paste its secret, into a repository or document.



Find your zone, then create an A record pointing <server> at the VM’s IP (Nectar: create a recordset):
openstack zone list
openstack recordset create <project>.cloud.edu.au. <server> --type A --record <ip>
openstack recordset list <project>.cloud.edu.au.
Note the trailing dot on the zone name. It is a fully qualified name and the commands fail without it.
Wait a minute or two, then check that the name resolves to your IP:
host <fqdn>
You can also create the record in the dashboard: Project → DNS → Zones → Create Record Set.




In the dashboard (Project → Network → Security Groups), add a group, e.g. http-https, with ingress rules for TCP 80 and TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and attach it to the instance. Port 80 is needed for the Let’s Encrypt challenge and the HTTP to HTTPS redirect.
The same from the command line:
openstack security group create http-https
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 80 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 http-https
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 443 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 http-https
openstack server add security group <server> http-https
Do not open 8787. If an old group allows it, remove that group from the instance:
openstack server remove security group <server> <group-with-8787>



sudo apt install nginx
Create /etc/nginx/sites-available/rstudio, based on Posit’s proxy configuration. Files in sites-available are included inside nginx’s http { } block, so don’t edit /etc/nginx/nginx.conf.
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/rstudio
# Support proxying of websocket connections (RStudio needs these)
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      close;
}

server {
  listen 80;
  listen [::]:80;
  server_name <fqdn>;

  # allow larger uploads through the RStudio Files pane
  client_max_body_size 100M;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_read_timeout 20d;
  }
}
Posit’s example uses proxy_set_header Host $host:$server_port; and says to leave out the port when serving on the default 80/443, so this uses $host. client_max_body_size is optional (nginx’s default is 1M).
Enable the site, disable the default one, test, and reload:
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/rstudio /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/rstudio
sudo rm /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
At this point http://<fqdn> should show the RStudio login page. Don’t log in yet, because it isn’t encrypted.



certbot.eff.org recommends installing certbot as a snap, and Ubuntu cloud images ship with snapd:
sudo apt remove certbot   # only if an old apt version is installed
sudo snap install --classic certbot
sudo ln -s /snap/bin/certbot /usr/local/bin/certbot
TODO(verify): that the Nectar Ubuntu 24.04 image includes snapd. If it doesn’t (or you’d rather avoid snaps), sudo apt install python3-certbot-nginx also works on 24.04, with a slightly older certbot.
Request the certificate and let certbot edit the nginx site:
sudo certbot --nginx -d <fqdn>
It asks for an email address (for expiry warnings) and for you to agree to the terms. If it asks about redirecting, choose redirect. TODO(verify): recent certbot seems to add the HTTP to HTTPS redirect without asking. If it doesn’t, add --redirect to the command. Afterwards the server block in /etc/nginx/sites-available/rstudio has listen 443 ssl and certificate lines marked # managed by Certbot, plus a second block that redirects port 80.
Renewal is automatic. The snap installs a systemd timer (the apt package does too), and certificates renew before they expire. Check it and do a dry run:
systemctl list-timers | grep -i certbot
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
Now open https://<fqdn>. http://<fqdn> should redirect there.



RStudio Server logs in with ordinary Linux accounts. For each person:
sudo adduser <username>
Give them a temporary password, sent separately from the username (e.g. by a different channel), and ask them to change it on first login:

Log in at https://<fqdn>.
Open the Terminal tab (Tools → Terminal → New Terminal) and run:
passwd
Choose a long, unique password, ideally from a password manager. Sign out and back in so the password manager saves the new one.

Don’t give users sudo unless they need it. See 08 for managing users over time. Never write real usernames, passwords, IP addresses or credential files into shared notes or this repo.



sudo nginx -t                              # config syntax
sudo journalctl -u nginx -e                # nginx service log
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log   # proxy errors (502 = RStudio not reachable)
sudo systemctl status rstudio-server
sudo rstudio-server verify-installation
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log

certbot fails the challenge: check that host <fqdn> returns your IP and that port 80 is open in the security group.
Login page loads but the session hangs or keeps disconnecting: the websocket Upgrade/Connection headers are missing from the nginx site.
502 Bad Gateway: RStudio Server isn’t running, or isn’t on 127.0.0.1:8787.




To serve RStudio at https://<fqdn>/rstudio/ with something else (a landing page, Jupyter) at /, see Posit’s proxy guide for the sub-path configuration. In outline, add this inside the existing server block, keeping the websocket headers from above:
location /rstudio/ {
  rewrite ^/rstudio/(.*)$ /$1 break;
  proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787;
  proxy_http_version 1.1;
  proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
  proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
  proxy_set_header Host $host;
  proxy_set_header X-RStudio-Root-Path /rstudio;
  proxy_read_timeout 20d;
}
The X-RStudio-Root-Path header and www-root-path=/rstudio in /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf do the same job, so you need only one. If both are set, the header wins.

It launches a VM with RStudio Server and Shiny Server already installed. If you choose a DNS zone during the deploy, you get automatic HTTPS at https://<host>.<project>.cloud.edu.au. You can also add a volume, which must be in the same availability zone as the VM (Nectar support: R-Studio application, tutorial: configuring applications).
Each deploy creates its own security group. Delete these when you delete the application, or they pile up (Nectar support: application security groups).
The rest of this page is the do-it-yourself route: more steps, but you choose the versions, the configuration and what else runs on the machine.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
A running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS VM you can SSH into as ubuntu (04). Ubuntu 26.04 LTS is supported by CRAN and Posit, so it should work the same way. TODO(verify): whether Nectar currently offers an official Ubuntu 26.04 image.
Your project has an allocation. Nectar creates a DNS zone named after the project (<project>.cloud.edu.au.) for new and renewed allocations (Nectar DNS service).

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
Follow CRAN’s Ubuntu instructions. On the VM:
sudo apt update -qq
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends software-properties-common dirmngr
wget -qO- https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/marutter_pubkey.asc \
  | sudo tee -a /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc
# optional: fingerprint should be E298A3A825C0D65DFD57CBB651716619E084DAB9
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc
sudo add-apt-repository "deb https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs)-cran40/"
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends r-base r-base-dev
$(lsb_release -cs) fills in your release (noble for 24.04, resolute for 26.04). For geospatial libraries and binary packages, see 07.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
Get the current Ubuntu .deb from Posit’s download page (it currently redirects to docs.posit.co/ide/user/download.html). The one package, built on jammy, is for Ubuntu 22, 24 and 26. Don’t copy a version number from old notes: the filename changes with every release.
Either copy the link from that page, or use Posit’s “latest stable” redirect and check which version it points to:
curl -sI https://rstudio.org/download/latest/stable/server/jammy/rstudio-server-latest-amd64.deb | grep -i ^location
Then download and install it (in October 2026 the current file was rstudio-server-2026.10.1-239-amd64.deb):
wget https://rstudio.org/download/latest/stable/server/jammy/rstudio-server-latest-amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./rstudio-server-latest-amd64.deb
sudo systemctl status rstudio-server
apt install ./file.deb pulls in dependencies, so you no longer need gdebi. TODO(verify): the rstudio.org/download/latest/... redirect is not documented on Posit’s download page, though it worked when this was written. If it stops working, copy the link from the download page instead.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
nginx will be the only way in, so tell RStudio Server not to listen on the public interface (Posit: running with a proxy):
echo "www-address=127.0.0.1" | sudo tee -a /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf
sudo systemctl restart rstudio-server
Check it:
sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8787
You should see 127.0.0.1:8787, not 0.0.0.0:8787.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
You do this with the OpenStack command-line client and its DNS (Designate) plugin. It can run on any machine, such as your laptop or the VM itself.


Use a venv rather than apt install python3-openstackclient. The apt packages can lag behind and mixing them with system Python caused trouble before (see issue #14). Ubuntu 24.04 also refuses pip install outside a venv.
sudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip
python3 -m venv ~/venvs/openstack
source ~/venvs/openstack/bin/activate
pip install python-openstackclient python-designateclient
When you come back later, run source ~/venvs/openstack/bin/activate again first. References: Nectar: OpenStack client, Python venv docs.



Do either of the following.
Application credential (preferred for anything scripted or left on a machine). In the Nectar dashboard, select the right project, then go to Identity → Application Credentials, create one, and download its openrc file. It is tied to one project, can be revoked, and doesn’t expose your personal password (Nectar: application credentials, using them).
# clear any leftover OS_* variables first, e.g. open a fresh shell
source app-cred-<name>-openrc.sh
Project OpenStack RC file. In the dashboard, select the project, click your email address (top right), and choose “OpenStack RC File”. You’ll be asked for your OpenStack password. This is not your institutional login: generate it under Settings → Reset Password (Nectar: credentials).
source <project>-openrc.sh
Never commit either file, or paste its secret, into a repository or document.



Find your zone, then create an A record pointing <server> at the VM’s IP (Nectar: create a recordset):
openstack zone list
openstack recordset create <project>.cloud.edu.au. <server> --type A --record <ip>
openstack recordset list <project>.cloud.edu.au.
Note the trailing dot on the zone name. It is a fully qualified name and the commands fail without it.
Wait a minute or two, then check that the name resolves to your IP:
host <fqdn>
You can also create the record in the dashboard: Project → DNS → Zones → Create Record Set.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
In the dashboard (Project → Network → Security Groups), add a group, e.g. http-https, with ingress rules for TCP 80 and TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and attach it to the instance. Port 80 is needed for the Let’s Encrypt challenge and the HTTP to HTTPS redirect.
The same from the command line:
openstack security group create http-https
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 80 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 http-https
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 443 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 http-https
openstack server add security group <server> http-https
Do not open 8787. If an old group allows it, remove that group from the instance:
openstack server remove security group <server> <group-with-8787>

6. RStudio Server
text:
certbot.eff.org recommends installing certbot as a snap, and Ubuntu cloud images ship with snapd:
sudo apt remove certbot   # only if an old apt version is installed
sudo snap install --classic certbot
sudo ln -s /snap/bin/certbot /usr/local/bin/certbot
TODO(verify): that the Nectar Ubuntu 24.04 image includes snapd. If it doesn’t (or you’d rather avoid snaps), sudo apt install python3-certbot-nginx also works on 24.04, with a slightly older certbot.
Request the certificate and let certbot edit the nginx site:
sudo certbot --nginx -d <fqdn>
It asks for an email address (for expiry warnings) and for you to agree to the terms. If it asks about redirecting, choose redirect. TODO(verify): recent certbot seems to add the HTTP to HTTPS redirect without asking. If it doesn’t, add --redirect to the command. Afterwards the server block in /etc/nginx/sites-available/rstudio has listen 443 ssl and certificate lines marked # managed by Certbot, plus a second block that redirects port 80.
Renewal is automatic. The snap installs a systemd timer (the apt package does too), and certificates renew before they expire. Check it and do a dry run:
systemctl list-timers | grep -i certbot
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
Now open https://<fqdn>. http://<fqdn> should redirect there.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
RStudio Server logs in with ordinary Linux accounts. For each person:
sudo adduser <username>
Give them a temporary password, sent separately from the username (e.g. by a different channel), and ask them to change it on first login:

Log in at https://<fqdn>.
Open the Terminal tab (Tools → Terminal → New Terminal) and run:
passwd
Choose a long, unique password, ideally from a password manager. Sign out and back in so the password manager saves the new one.

Don’t give users sudo unless they need it. See 08 for managing users over time. Never write real usernames, passwords, IP addresses or credential files into shared notes or this repo.

title: 6. RStudio Server
text:
sudo nginx -t                              # config syntax
sudo journalctl -u nginx -e                # nginx service log
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log   # proxy errors (502 = RStudio not reachable)
sudo systemctl status rstudio-server
sudo rstudio-server verify-installation
sudo tail -n 50 /var/log/letsencrypt/letsencrypt.log

certbot fails the challenge: check that host <fqdn> returns your IP and that port 80 is open in the security group.
Login page loads but the session hangs or keeps disconnecting: the websocket Upgrade/Connection headers are missing from the nginx site.
502 Bad Gateway: RStudio Server isn’t running, or isn’t on 127.0.0.1:8787.

4. Launch a VM
text:
Status: draft. Checked against Nectar support and tutorial pages, October 2026.

The details behind the six steps on the front page. They take you from nothing to logging in to your own Ubuntu VM. Steps 3 and 4 are done once per project; after that, each new VM is one launch.
Nothing here is precious. If a VM doesn’t work, delete it and launch another.
Placeholders: <ip> is the VM’s public IP address, <az> is an availability zone, <name> is the instance name or a username (each step says which).


Go to the dashboard, choose Login via AAF (Australia) or Login via Tuakiri (New Zealand), and use your university login. More, including what to do if your organisation isn’t in AAF: Your allocation.



The project menu at the top left shows which project you’re working in. After your first login it’s your Project Trial, pt-NNNN: up to 4 cores, for 6 months (details). Project > Compute > Overview shows how much of its quota is in use.
If you’ve been given a different project, choose it from that menu.



Nectar images have no default passwords. You log in with an SSH key (Nectar: keypairs).

On your own computer (Linux, macOS, or Windows PowerShell, which includes OpenSSH), run:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
Accept the default location (~/.ssh/id_ed25519, or C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\id_ed25519 on Windows) and set a passphrase.
In the dashboard, go to Project > Compute > Key Pairs > Import Public Key. Give the key a name and paste in the contents of id_ed25519.pub. Paste the .pub file, never the private key.

The private key (id_ed25519, no .pub) stays on your computer. Don’t email it, copy it to shared drives, or commit it anywhere. If you lose it, you can’t log in to VMs launched with it: make a new key and launch new VMs.
On Windows, MobaXterm is an alternative with a built-in terminal, SSH client and file browser. It can use the same key.



A security group is a firewall rule set attached to an instance. Inbound traffic is blocked unless a rule allows it. Rules add up across groups, and outbound traffic is open (Nectar: security groups).
An allocated project starts with one group, default. It has no inbound rules and is shared by every member of the project, so don’t add rules to it. Create your own groups instead (Project > Network > Security Groups > Create Security Group, then Manage Rules > Add Rule; Nectar tutorial):








Group
Rule
Remote (CIDR)




ssh
SSH (TCP 22)
ideally your institution’s network range rather than 0.0.0.0/0


http
HTTP (TCP 80)
0.0.0.0/0


https
HTTPS (TCP 443)
0.0.0.0/0



You only need http and https if the VM serves web pages, such as RStudio Server behind nginx (06).
Never open port 8787 (RStudio Server) to the world. Logins would cross the network unencrypted. 06 puts RStudio behind HTTPS instead.
A Project Trial (pt-NNNN) comes with ready-made SSH, HTTP and ICMP groups, so there you can skip this step and just pick the SSH group at launch.



Go to Project > Compute > Instances > Launch Instance (Nectar tutorial). Work through the dialog’s tabs:

Details: an instance name (<name>), and the availability zone. “Any Availability Zone” is fine, unless you’ll attach a volume. A volume can only attach to an instance in the same zone, so pick that zone here (see 05). Some allocations are limited to one node’s zones.
Source: Boot Source “Image”. Filter for and select NeCTAR Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble) amd64. The Nectar tutorials still show 20.04, which is out of standard support, so don’t copy it. A 26.04 image is in Nectar’s image build repo. TODO(verify): whether 26.04 appears in the dashboard yet. If asked “Create New Volume”, choose No unless you want a volume-backed root disk (it uses volume quota; see 05).
Flavour: pick a size that fits your quota (see 03), e.g. m3.small in a Project Trial, or m3.medium.
Networks: Classic Provider. This gives the instance a public IPv4 address directly (Nectar: classic vs advanced networking).
Security Groups: add ssh (and http, https if needed). You can leave default attached, because it adds nothing inbound.
Key Pair: select the key you imported. Don’t skip this. The key is put on the VM when it’s first created, so a VM launched without one can’t be logged in to. Delete it and launch again.

Click Launch Instance. The status goes from Build to Active in a minute or two.



The IP is in the IP Address column of Project > Compute > Instances. From your own computer:
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ubuntu@<ip>
The first time, SSH asks you to confirm the host’s fingerprint. Type yes. If it says “Connection refused” or times out, wait a minute (the VM may still be booting) and check that the ssh group is attached and allows your network.
The login user depends on the image (Nectar: images):



Image
User




Ubuntu
ubuntu


Debian
debian


Rocky Linux
rocky


AlmaLinux
almalinux


Fedora
fedora


CentOS (old)
ec2-user







Update everything, then reboot:
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade
sudo reboot
Wait a minute and log in again.
Create a normal user for yourself (and one for each other person):
sudo adduser <name>
Add sudo usermod -aG sudo <name> only for people who administer the machine.
To let that user log in over SSH with your key, copy it across:
sudo mkdir -p /home/<name>/.ssh
sudo cp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/<name>/.ssh/
sudo chown -R <name>:<name> /home/<name>/.ssh
sudo chmod 700 /home/<name>/.ssh
Each person should really use their own key: append their .pub to their own authorized_keys.

Next: storage (05), RStudio Server (06), software (07).



After you’ve done this a few times, the OpenStack client is quicker and easy to script. It runs on your laptop (Windows: use WSL) or on another VM.


Use a Python virtual environment (Nectar: OpenStack client):
python3 -m venv ~/venvs/openstack
source ~/venvs/openstack/bin/activate
pip install python-openstackclient
Run source ~/venvs/openstack/bin/activate again in each new shell.




Application credential (preferred). In the dashboard, select the project, then Identity > Application Credentials > Create. Download the openrc file (or clouds.yaml). It is tied to one project, can be revoked, and doesn’t expose your password (Nectar: application credentials).
source app-cred-<name>-openrc.sh
# or, with clouds.yaml in ~/.config/openstack/:
export OS_CLOUD=openstack
Project RC file. Click your email address (top right) > OpenStack RC File. It prompts for your OpenStack password, which is separate from your institutional login: set it under Settings > Reset Password (Nectar: credentials).

Start from a fresh shell, or unset any old OS_* variables, so that two sets of credentials don’t mix. Never commit these files to a repository.



openstack server list
openstack flavor list
openstack image list --property owner=28eadf5ad64b42a4929b2fb7df99275c   # official Nectar images
openstack availability zone list
openstack keypair list
openstack security group list
The owner ID is Nectar’s Public-Images project (Nectar: images). To narrow the list, add --name "NeCTAR Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble) amd64".



openstack security group create ssh
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 22 --remote-ip <your-cidr> ssh
openstack security group create https
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 443 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 https
Do the same for http with port 80.



openstack keypair create --public-key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub <keyname>

openstack server create \
  --image "NeCTAR Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble) amd64" \
  --flavor m3.medium \
  --network "Classic Provider" \
  --key-name <keyname> \
  --security-group ssh \
  --availability-zone <az> \
  <name>
Repeat --security-group for each group. Leave out --availability-zone if you don’t need a particular zone. Nectar’s CLI tutorial doesn’t include a server create example; these are the standard OpenStack client options. TODO(verify): run this against Nectar and confirm the network name Classic Provider is accepted as written.
Then get the IP and log in:
openstack server show <name> -c status -c addresses
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ubuntu@<ip>




A VM that is shut off still uses your SU budget. Only shelving or deleting it stops the use (Nectar: Service Units). If a VM will sit idle for weeks:
openstack server shelve <name>     # saves it as a snapshot and frees the resources
openstack server unshelve <name>   # brings it back later
(Dashboard: the instance’s Actions menu > Shelve Instance.) Unshelving takes a few minutes. TODO(verify): whether a Classic Provider instance keeps its IP address after unshelving. If it changes, update any DNS record (06).
Delete a VM you no longer need, after saving anything on it. See 08 for snapshots, shelving and handing a machine back.

title: 2. Your allocation
text:
Status: draft

How to get your own Nectar resources: the Project Trial you get at first login, then applying for a bigger allocation when you need one.
If your group already runs a Nectar project, its manager can add you as a member instead; ask them how they do it.



Go to the dashboard and choose Login via AAF (Australia) or Login via Tuakiri (New Zealand), then use your university credentials (logging in).
Not sure you’re eligible? Use the eligibility checker (about). If your organisation isn’t in AAF, a collaborator’s institution or an AAF Virtual Home account may work (no AAF).
Your account goes inactive after 6 months without a login; logging in again reactivates it.




Your first login creates a Project Trial (pt-NNNN): up to 4 vCPU, expiring after 6 months, and not shareable (Project Trial, tutorial). The tutorial describes the budget as “4 vCPU for up to 6 vCPU-months”. A shut-off instance still counts; only shelving or deleting stops it. A trial is fine for learning how to launch a VM (04-launch-a-vm.md), but it has no DNS name and is too small for most real work.




Link your ORCID first; the form won’t go through without it (ORCID).
In the dashboard, Allocations > New Request. You can convert your Project Trial into the new project (it keeps whatever you’ve built, and you get a fresh empty trial) or start a new project (converting).
Choose a Resource Bundle (bundles):



Bundle
Service Units per year




Standard
4,000


Powerful
8,000


Extreme
16,000

title: 2. Your allocation
Need a bigger computer?
text:
The ARDC Nectar Research Cloud lets Australian researchers create their own virtual machines (VMs): computers in a data centre that you start, log in to, install what you like on, and delete when you’re done. It’s free for researchers, and it sits between your laptop and a supercomputer.
This page is a short way in, and a list of places to go next.

Status: early draft. The old notes this grew out of are in legacy/.



Probably, if:

your laptop is too slow, too small, or you need something running overnight or for weeks;
you want a machine you control: your own software, your own users, always on;
you want to serve something on the web (RStudio Server, Jupyter, marimo, Shiny, a website, a data service), or to work on a remote machine from Positron or VS Code over SSH;
you use HPC but want something interactive alongside it.

If you have a university email address (.edu.au), try logging in now: go to the Nectar dashboard and choose Login via AAF. If it works, you already have a small personal allocation (a Project Trial) and can launch a VM today. Not sure you’re eligible? Use the eligibility checker.
The trial is small (up to 4 cores, for 6 months). When you need more, you apply for your own allocation. How to think about that, and how big a machine you need:

Your allocation: the trial, applying, renewing, what happens at expiry
Sizing: how big a machine is, and turning that into Service Units
The words: project, allocation, flavour, image, instance, volume




Six steps. Each one has a “more” link if you get stuck; otherwise just do it. Nothing here is precious. If something goes wrong, delete the VM and start again.

Log in to the dashboard with AAF. More
Check your allocation. Your Project Trial (pt-NNNN) is selected at the top left. More
Create a keypair, and save the private key. This is how you’ll log in; there are no passwords. More
Allow SSH in. A security group is a firewall rule. Without one that allows SSH you can see your VM but not reach it. More
Launch an instance. Pick an image (Ubuntu), a flavour (size), your security group, and your key. A VM launched without a key can’t be logged in to; delete it and launch another. More
Connect with SSH: ssh ubuntu@<ip>. More

That’s it: you have a computer.
Next: put something on the web. RStudio Server behind HTTPS with a proper name, or the dashboard’s one-click “Quick Deploy” for RStudio.
Once you’re using it:

Storage: volumes, object storage, network mounts
Software: R and geospatial stacks, containers, Python
Looking after it: users, updates, snapshots, shelving, handing it back






Same idea, different deal. Nectar runs OpenStack, and most EC2 words have a direct match: instance type → flavour, AMI → image, EBS → volume, S3 → object storage (Nectar’s has an S3-compatible API), and security groups and keypairs are the same. The differences are that Nectar is free to eligible researchers, paid for with an allocation of Service Units instead of a credit card, and it has no managed databases, queues or serverless: you get VMs, storage and DNS. More



HPC (supercomputers and university clusters) is for big batch jobs: you submit work to a queue, it runs across many cores, and the centre looks after the software. A Nectar VM is yours. It’s interactive, always on, you have root, and you maintain it (ARDC: cloud vs HPC). Many people use both. If you have an HPC project, interactive work is possible there too: NCI’s ARE runs RStudio and Jupyter in the browser, and both NCI and Pawsey document running them inside a job. More

NCI: Gadi, the national supercomputer
Pawsey: Setonix, and since December 2025 also a Nectar node
Monash: a Nectar node and  university HPC
QCIF: runs the Queensland Nectar node (QRIScloud) for UQ, QUT and other Queensland members, and brokers HPC access
Your own university’s research computing team, who often run a cluster and can help with a Nectar allocation




Nectar is run by partner organisations (“nodes”), each with its own data centre. Your institution’s node can approve local allocations; national allocations are approved centrally and can run anywhere. The nodes are Intersect (NSW), Queensland, Adelaide, Tasmania, Melbourne Research Cloud, Monash, Swinburne, Pawsey, National (ARDC-AARNet), and Auckland (NZ) (current list and members).

title: 1. Concepts
text:
Status: draft

The few words you need before anything else makes sense. You don’t need to memorise them; come back here when a later page uses one.





Word
What it means




Cloud
Computers that aren’t on your desk, and that you create for yourself when you need them. They run the same kind of software as your laptop, but you reach them over the network. On Nectar the cloud software is called OpenStack.


Project
The shared account that owns resources in Nectar. People are members of projects. (Older pages call it a “tenant”.)


Allocation
Your request for resources, and its approval. It gives a project a quota for a period of up to 12 months, and can be renewed.


Project Trial
A small personal project (named like pt-12345) created the first time you log in. Up to 4 vCPU, expires after 6 months, and can’t be shared with anyone else. Good for trying things out.


Resource Bundle
The pre-set sizes you choose from when you apply: Standard, Powerful, Extreme or Custom. Each comes with a yearly budget of Service Units plus limits on cores, RAM, and so on.


Service Units (SU)
The “currency” of an allocation. Every machine size costs a fixed number of SU per hour while it exists. When your SU run out, the allocation expires.


Quota
The limits that come with an allocation: how many cores (vCPU), how much RAM, how many instances, how much volume and object storage.


Flavour
A machine size: cores, RAM and root disk, e.g. m3.large (8 cores, 16 GB RAM). See 03-sizing.md.


Image
The operating system you start from, usually an official Nectar Ubuntu image such as NeCTAR Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble) amd64.


Instance (VM)
A running machine, built from an image at a flavour, inside a project. “VM” means virtual machine; it behaves like a real computer that you have to yourself.


Volume
An extra, persistent disk you attach to one instance at a time. It survives when the instance is deleted, which the instance’s own root disk does not.


Object storage
A place to keep files (as “objects” in “containers”) that you reach over the web rather than as a disk, a bit like Dropbox. Good for sharing and for big read-mostly data. Not backed up.


Snapshot
A saved copy of an instance’s root disk, or of a volume. You can launch new instances from an instance snapshot.


Availability zone / node
Nectar is run by several partner organisations (“nodes”), each with its own data centre(s), called availability zones (e.g. tasmania, melbourne-qh2). A volume and the instance it attaches to must be in the same availability zone.



Sources: project, allocations, Project Trial, Resource Bundles, Service Units, flavours, object storage.



From legacy/README-2014.md, and still true:

Snapshot: set a machine up once, save it, and launch copies of it.
Recipe: a script (or container) that turns a clean machine into a working one.

They aren’t mutually exclusive. Recipes age better: a snapshot freezes an old operating system and old software, while a recipe can be re-run on next year’s image. Keep a recipe even if you also keep snapshots.



Nectar runs OpenStack, which does much the same job as EC2. Most of what you know carries across:



AWS
Nectar (OpenStack)




Account, billed by card
Project, with an allocation of Service Units (free to eligible researchers)


Instance type (t3.large)
Flavour (m3.large)


AMI
Image


EBS volume
Volume (Cinder)


S3
Object storage (Swift), with an S3-compatible API


Security group, key pair
Same names, same idea


Elastic IP
Floating IP (only with Advanced networking; most VMs get a public IP directly)


Region / availability zone
Node / availability zone (e.g. tasmania, melbourne-qh2)


Route 53
DNS (Designate): a <project>.cloud.edu.au zone for allocated projects


aws CLI
openstack CLI


User data, instance metadata
Same: cloud-init reads user data, and 169.254.169.254 serves EC2-style metadata



What Nectar doesn’t have: managed databases, queues, serverless, autoscaling, or a marketplace beyond a handful of ready-made applications. You get VMs, storage, and networking, and you build the rest. Nor is there a bill that grows with use: when the Service Units run out, the allocation expires.













Your desktop/laptop
Nectar cloud VM
HPC (NCI Gadi, Pawsey Setonix, university cluster)




How you work
Interactive
Interactive (RStudio, Jupyter, a terminal), or long jobs left running
Batch: you submit jobs to a queue and wait


Always on?
Only while it’s on and awake
Yes, until you shelve or delete it
Jobs run when the scheduler lets them; there’s a time limit


Root/admin access
Usually
Yes: it’s your machine, you install what you like
No; software via modules or containers


Who maintains it
You or your IT
You (updates, users, security)
The HPC centre


How you get access
Buy it
Join a project or apply for an allocation (free to Australian researchers)
Apply for a compute allocation through your institution or a national scheme


Typical size
4–16 cores, 8–64 GB RAM
1–32 cores (64 on c3), up to 128 GB RAM; bigger by special request
Thousands of cores, many nodes per job



In short: HPC is for massive or highly parallel jobs; the cloud is for on-demand, interactive, always-on work that you control (ARDC: cloud computing, support: cloud vs HPC). The Nectar tutorial “What is cloud?” has a “do I need it?” checklist: more compute, sharing with collaborators, hosting a service, a different operating system, or work that runs for a long time.


If you only need a bit more than your laptop for a few days or weeks, these managed services work with just a Nectar login (eligibility and services):

Virtual Desktop Service: a Linux desktop in your browser, 8 cores / 16 GB RAM (boost to 16 / 32), for 14 days at a time, extendable (details). How long it stays shelved before deletion differs between pages (30 days, 1 month or 3 months): TODO(verify).
Jupyter Notebook Service: notebooks in the browser, nothing to install.
BinderHub: run a notebook straight from a Git repository.

For GPU and AI work, look at the National GPU Service rather than a general VM.

title: 3. Sizing
text:
Status: draft

Two questions: how big is the machine you have now, and how big does the new one need to be? Then turn the answer into Service Units for your request.




On a Linux machine (or a Mac, for some of these), open a terminal and type:
nproc                                          # number of CPU cores
free -h                                        # RAM ("total" column)
df -h                                          # disk size and usage per filesystem
lsblk                                          # disks and volumes attached
cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep 'model name' | head -1   # CPU model
If the machine is a Nectar VM, it can tell you about itself through the OpenStack metadata service (OpenStack docs):
# the instance's name, availability zone and project ID
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/openstack/latest/meta_data.json

# the flavour name, e.g. m3.large (EC2-style metadata)
curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-type
meta_data.json does not include the flavour; the instance-type path should. TODO(verify) both on a current Nectar VM.




Project > Compute > Overview: pie charts of how much of your project’s quota (instances, vCPU, RAM, volumes) is in use.
Project > Compute > Instances: each instance’s flavour, IP address and availability zone. Click an instance’s name for details.
Usage menu: Service Units used over time, and how many are left (usage graphs).





A flavour name is family.size. The general-purpose families (flavours, Aug 2026):

The sizes go xsmall, small, medium, large, xlarge, xxlarge, each doubling the cores and RAM of the one before (e.g. m3.medium = 4 vCPU/8 GB, m3.large = 8/16).
Other things to know:

No ephemeral disk on these standard flavours: you get only the root disk (30 GB, or 10 GB on t3). Data goes on a volume (05-storage.md). Only the reserved GPU (g1, g2, g3) and huge-RAM (h4) flavours come with ephemeral disk.
Node-private flavours exist at some nodes, e.g. tas.c16m64 at Tasmania (16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM). They’re arranged with the node by support ticket, and their naming and SU rates aren’t documented centrally: TODO(verify) with the node.

Sources: root disk and boot sources, flavours, Resource Bundles, object storage overview, Manila.
Standard flavours have no separate ephemeral disk; only some GPU and huge-memory flavours do.
Rule of thumb: treat the root disk as disposable. Keep code in git, data on a volume or in object storage, and your setup as a script (08).





Volume storage is not part of the Resource Bundles. Request it as a Location Specific Resource in your allocation request (or an amendment, Dashboard → Allocations → My Requests → Amend), for a specific availability zone, e.g. tasmania or melbourne-qh2. Ask for it in the same availability zone you will run your VM in. See 02 and the Resource Bundles page.
Check your quota at Project → Volumes → Overview, or:
openstack quota show --volume
TODO(verify): exact flag; openstack quota show without flags also lists volume gigabytes.



Following the Nectar volume tutorial:

Find your instance’s availability zone: Project → Compute → Instances → click the instance.
Project → Volumes → Volumes → Create Volume. Give it a name, a size in GB, and the same availability zone as the instance. A volume in another zone can’t be attached.
In the volume’s dropdown, Manage Attachments → choose the instance → Attach.

Or from the command line:
openstack volume create --size 500 --availability-zone <zone> <volname>
openstack server add volume <server> <volname>

On the VM, see the new disk:
lsblk
It usually appears as /dev/vdb or /dev/vdc, with no mount point. Check the size matches what you created.





Warning: mkfs erases everything on the device. Only do this to a brand new, empty volume. If you are re-attaching a volume that already holds data, skip to Mount.

If you’re not sure, check for an existing filesystem first:
sudo blkid /dev/vdc        # prints TYPE="ext4" etc. if it is already formatted
No output means no filesystem. Then:
sudo mkfs -t ext4 /dev/vdc



This guide mounts volumes at /mnt/data/<name> (e.g. /mnt/data/project, as used in 07). The Nectar tutorial uses /pvol; either works, just be consistent.

Make the mount point:
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/data/project
Get the volume’s UUID:
sudo blkid /dev/vdc
# /dev/vdc: UUID="3f1c...-...." BLOCK_SIZE="4096" TYPE="ext4"
Add a line to /etc/fstab (sudo nano /etc/fstab):
UUID=3f1c...-....  /mnt/data/project  ext4  defaults,nofail  0  2
Use the UUID rather than /dev/vdc: device names can change when you attach volumes in a different order, the UUID doesn’t. nofail lets the VM boot even if the volume isn’t attached. (The Nectar tutorial uses /dev/vdc /pvol auto defaults,nofail 0 2.)
Mount everything in fstab, and check:
sudo mount -a
df -h /mnt/data/project
If mount -a reports an error, fix /etc/fstab before you reboot.
Make it yours (or a group’s):
sudo chown ubuntu:ubuntu /mnt/data/project
For several users, create a group and give it the directory:
sudo groupadd lab
sudo usermod -aG lab <username>
sudo chgrp lab /mnt/data/project
sudo chmod 2775 /mnt/data/project   # setgid: new files inherit the group




Always in this order (Nectar tutorial):

Stop anything using it (RStudio sessions, containers), then unmount:
sudo umount /mnt/data/project
“target is busy” means something still has files open; sudo lsof +f -- /mnt/data/project shows what.
Comment out its line in /etc/fstab if it is not coming back.
Detach: Project → Volumes → Manage Attachments → Detach, or openstack server remove volume <server> <volname>.
Delete, only if you are sure: Project → Volumes → Delete Volume. This is irreversible. A volume with snapshots can’t be deleted until the snapshots are.

To move a volume to another VM, do steps 1 to 3, attach it to the new VM (same availability zone), and mount it. Don’t format it.



Volumes can grow, not shrink (Nectar tutorial):

Unmount and detach (above).
Project → Volumes → Extend Volume, enter the new size (needs quota), or openstack volume set --size <new-GB> <volname>.
Re-attach, then grow the filesystem before mounting:
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/vdc
sudo resize2fs /dev/vdc
sudo mount -a
df -h /mnt/data/project




A volume is not backed up by default. Nectar offers a volume backup service at all nodes:
openstack volume backup create --name project-2026-10 --force <volname>
openstack volume backup list
--force allows backing up an attached volume; for a consistent copy, unmount first. TODO(verify): whether backups need their own quota, and where they are stored.
A volume snapshot is not a backup: it lives on the same storage and uses volume quota equal to the volume’s size (08).




Object storage holds files (“objects”) in containers (S3 calls them buckets), reached over HTTPS from anywhere, not just your VM. Good for sharing results, staging inputs, and keeping copies off the VM. It is replicated across three availability zones but not backed up: a deleted object is gone (overview). There is no server-side encryption (support).


Following the Nectar S3 tutorial:

With the OpenStack client set up for your project (04), create EC2-style credentials:
openstack ec2 credentials create
Keep the access and secret values in a password manager. Anyone with them can read and write your project’s object storage. List or revoke with openstack ec2 credentials list / openstack ec2 credentials delete <access>.
Install rclone (sudo apt install rclone, or the newer build from rclone.org) and add this to ~/.config/rclone/rclone.conf (rclone config file shows the path):
[nectar_s3]
type = s3
provider = Other
endpoint = https://object-store.rc.nectar.org.au
access_key_id = <access>
secret_access_key = <secret>
Use it:
rclone mkdir nectar_s3:my-bucket
rclone copy /mnt/data/project/results nectar_s3:my-bucket/results --progress
rclone ls nectar_s3:my-bucket

Nectar doesn’t support S3 v4 streaming (“aws-chunked”) uploads. rclone works with its defaults; if any S3 client fails with a signature or authorisation error on upload, look for an option to turn off chunked/streaming uploads, or add v2_auth = true to the rclone remote.
Other S3 tools work with the same endpoint, e.g. aws --endpoint-url https://object-store.rc.nectar.org.au s3 ls, and so do GDAL (/vsis3/ with AWS_S3_ENDPOINT=object-store.rc.nectar.org.au) and R packages built on it. TODO(verify): GDAL may also need AWS_VIRTUAL_HOSTING=FALSE.



The native Swift client uses your OpenStack credentials directly:
pip install python-swiftclient
swift list                          # containers
swift upload my-container results/  # upload a directory
swift download my-container         # download a container
The dashboard (Project → Object Store → Containers) is fine for small files and for making a container public.




Some groups make large data collections available to VMs by network mount (e.g. NFS or SMB), so you can read them without copying. Access is arranged case by case with the collection’s maintainers, not through Nectar. Expect to need:

the VM’s IP address registered with them;
the right security group on the VM (outbound traffic is open by default, but some protocols need inbound rules too);
possibly a VPN, a key or credentials;
the VM in a particular availability zone, close to the data.

Ask the maintainers for the mount details, then add the mount to /etc/fstab with nofail as above, so the VM still boots if the share is unreachable.
Manila shared filesystems (Monash and Auckland only) are mounted the same way; see the Nectar Manila article.

7. Software
text:
Status: draft

There are three ways to get software onto your VM. They’re listed from least to most systematic. Most people should start with the first, move to the second when they want a ready-made environment, and only use the third when library versions really matter.

Install on the VM: apt, CRAN and a Python venv. Quick, familiar, and good enough for most work.
Containers: a ready-made image (rocker) run with Docker. Reproducible and disposable.
A systematic dependency stack: images in which GDAL, PROJ and GEOS are aligned across R and Python.

All commands assume the Nectar Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (“noble”) image and a user with sudo.




Ubuntu’s own r-base falls behind. CRAN’s Ubuntu repository has the current R release for 22.04, 24.04 and 26.04, on both amd64 and arm64 (CRAN: Ubuntu packages for R):
sudo apt update -qq
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends software-properties-common dirmngr
# Michael Rutter's signing key for the CRAN Ubuntu repository
wget -qO- https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu/marutter_pubkey.asc \
  | sudo tee -a /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc
sudo add-apt-repository "deb https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs)-cran40/"
sudo apt install --no-install-recommends r-base r-base-dev
To check the key, run the command below. The fingerprint should be E298A3A825C0D65DFD57CBB651716619E084DAB9.
gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/cran_ubuntu_key.asc

  ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python:dev
To build spatial packages in the overlay against the image’s GDAL, install them from source and stop pak from pulling in apt’s GDAL (the README’s “dual GDAL” problem):
options(pkg.sysreqs = FALSE)
pak::pkg_install("hypertidy/vapour?source")
To use JupyterLab from the browser, bind it to localhost and reach it through an SSH tunnel or the nginx proxy from section 6:
docker run --rm -ti \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8888:8888 \
  -v /mnt/data/project:/workspace \
  ghcr.io/hypertidy/gdal-r-python:latest \
  jupyter lab --ip=0.0.0.0 --port=8888 --allow-root --no-browser
TODO(verify): the JupyterLab command above has not been tested against the current image. The containers run as root, so files written to /workspace will be owned by root on the host. Consider --user $(id -u):$(id -g) (untested; HOME and venv permissions may need care).

title: 7. Software
text: Your group may maintain its own pathway: a shared VM image, an internal container registry, a package list, or a set of setup scripts. If so, document it here. Say what it provides, who maintains it, how to request access, and how it relates to the three pathways above. Open a pull request or an issue on this repository to add it.
